title: State Management at Scale
summary: Once prop drilling stops scaling, Context and external stores solve the reach problem in different ways with different re-render costs. Normalized state shape is what keeps either option correct as an app grows.

slides.markdown:
[State Management Fundamentals](state-management-fundamentals) ended with a checklist: lift state to the lowest common ancestor that needs it. That works cleanly for two or three components. It breaks down when the components that need a value are far apart in the tree — a theme toggle in a header and a chart deep inside a dashboard, a logged-in user's id needed by a dozen unrelated features.

At that point, "lift it further" means threading a value through every intermediate component that doesn't use it — pure **prop drilling**. This topic covers the two mainstream answers: **Context**, built into the framework for exactly this reach problem, and **external stores** (Redux, Zustand, Pinia-style patterns), which add a single source of truth outside the component tree entirely.

Both solve reach. They differ sharply in re-render cost, debuggability, and how much ceremony they demand — which is the actual decision interviewers are probing for, not "which one is better."

slides.subTitle: Prop-drilling pain
slides.markdown:
Prop drilling is what happens when a value's owner and its consumer are far apart in the tree, so the value has to be passed as a prop through every component in between — components that never read the value themselves, they only forward it.

This is a **maintainability** problem more than a performance one at first: every intermediate component's prop signature grows to include values it doesn't care about, renaming the value means touching every file in the chain, and adding a new consumer three levels deeper means threading the prop through three more components that have nothing to do with it.

The practical trigger for reaching past prop lifting isn't a fixed number of levels — it's **whether the intermediate components genuinely have no other reason to know about the value.** A theme, the logged-in user, a feature flag, and a global toast queue are classic candidates: broadly needed, rarely related to what any specific intermediate component actually does.

slides.sectionTitle: Context: solving reach, at a re-render cost
slides.markdown:
Context lets a component higher in the tree provide a value that any descendant can read directly, with no props threaded through the components in between — `useContext(ThemeContext)` reads the value regardless of how many layers separate the provider from the consumer.

The cost that catches people off guard: **every component consuming a Context re-renders whenever that Context's value changes**, even if the consumer only cares about one field of a larger value object. Put `{ user, theme, featureFlags }` in one Context, and a component that only reads `theme` still re-renders every time `user` changes, because React can't tell your components apart by which field they actually use — it only knows the Context object as a whole changed.

This is why Context is a strong fit for values that change **rarely** (theme, locale, auth state) and a poor fit for anything that changes on every keystroke or every render — for that, an external store's more granular subscription model, covered next, is the better tool.

slides.sectionTitle: External stores: single source of truth, actions and reducers
slides.markdown:
Redux-style (and Zustand/Pinia-style) stores move state entirely **outside** the component tree, into one plain object that any component can read from and any component can request changes to, via explicit **actions**.

The shape, in Redux's classic form:

- **Store**: one object holding the entire app's shared state.
- **Action**: a plain object describing what happened — `{ type: "cart/itemAdded", payload: { id: 42 } }` — not what should change, just a fact.
- **Reducer**: a pure function `(state, action) => newState` that computes the next state from the current state and the action, with no side effects.
- **Dispatch**: the only way to request a change — components call `dispatch(action)`, never mutate the store directly.

The payoff over Context: components subscribe to **specific slices** of the store (via a selector), so a component reading only `cart.items` re-renders only when that slice changes, not whenever any unrelated part of the store updates — the granular subscription Context can't offer natively.

slides.subTitle: Avoiding nested and duplicated data

slides.markdown:
| | Context | External store (Redux/Zustand-style) |
|---|---|
| **Best for** | rarely-changing, broadly-needed values (theme, locale, current user) | frequently-changing, structured app state (cart, entity cache, form wizards) |
| **Re-render granularity** | every consumer re-renders on any value change | subscribers re-render only when their selected slice changes |
| **Setup cost** | built into the framework, minimal boilerplate | extra dependency, more upfront structure (actions/reducers or store definitions) |
| **Debuggability** | value is just whatever was provided — no built-in history | many stores ship devtools with full action history and time-travel |

The practical rule: reach for Context first for anything that changes rarely and is needed broadly; reach for a store once state changes frequently, needs granular subscriptions to avoid re-render cost, or benefits from a single, inspectable log of every change (which matters a great deal when debugging "why did this value change" in a large app).

slides.sectionTitle: Putting everything in global state "just in case"
slides.markdown:
The over-correction after learning about Context or stores: moving state that's genuinely local — a form's in-progress draft, a modal's open flag, a single component's expanded/collapsed toggle — into global state "in case something else needs it later."

This has a real cost, not just a stylistic one: global state has to be explicit about ownership and update paths (an action, a reducer case, a Context update function) even for state nothing outside one component actually touches, which adds indirection with zero benefit. It also widens the **blast radius** of a bug — a mistake in a globally-shared reducer can affect every component reading that store, where the same mistake in one component's local state would have been contained to that component alone.

The same checklist from [State Management Fundamentals](state-management-fundamentals) still applies at this scale: default to local, lift only as far as the actual consumers require, and reach for Context or a store only when the reach genuinely crosses the tree in a way prop lifting can't reasonably solve — not preemptively.

A practical fix for Context's all-consumers-re-render cost, used constantly in real codebases: split one large Context object into **several smaller Contexts**, one per concern that changes independently.

Instead of a single `AppContext` holding `{ user, theme, featureFlags }`, provide `UserContext`, `ThemeContext`, and `FeatureFlagContext` separately. A component that only reads `useContext(ThemeContext)` now only re-renders when the theme itself changes — a `user` update updates a completely different Context and never touches this component at all.

This is a cheap, framework-native mitigation that closes most of the practical gap with a store's granular subscriptions, for the cases where you'd otherwise reach for a full store purely to fix Context's re-render cost rather than because you actually need actions, reducers, or middleware.

The reach problem and its two solution families exist in every mainstream framework, under different names:

| Concept | React | Vue | Angular |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reach without drilling** | Context (`useContext`) | `provide`/`inject` | dependency injection via services |
| **Structured external store** | Redux, Zustand | Pinia | NgRx, or a shared injectable service |
| **Granular subscription** | store selectors | Pinia's reactive refs (fine-grained by default) | RxJS observables/selectors |

Vue's `provide`/`inject` is the direct sibling of Context, with the same all-consumers-react caveat unless the provided value itself is fine-grained reactive. Angular leans on its dependency-injection system plus RxJS observables for the same job — an injectable service is effectively a store, and components subscribe to just the observable slices they need, which sidesteps the Context-style blanket re-render problem by design.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing the state layer for a shared board
slides.markdown:
A strong answer to "design the state layer for a Trello-like board" walks through ownership and shape before naming a tool:

1. **Normalize first.** Boards, lists, and cards are entities with relationships — store them flat, keyed by id (`cards.byId`, `lists.byId`), with lists referencing card ids and cards referencing a list id, rather than nesting cards inside lists inside boards.
2. **Separate server-cache state from client-only state.** "Which cards exist and what they contain" is server data that needs caching/invalidation semantics; "which card is being dragged right now" or "is this modal open" is transient client state that doesn't belong in the same store, if not the same category of tool at all.
3. **Pick reach, not preference.** A drag-in-progress position only needs to reach the board and the card being dragged — that's local or lifted state, not a global store entry. Which board/list/card data exists needs to reach nearly every component on the screen — that's store territory.
4. **Subscribe granularly.** A single card component should re-render when *its own* data changes, not when any card anywhere on the board changes — which is exactly the selector-based subscription a store gives you and a single flat Context wouldn't.

Naming the normalization and the reach-based ownership decision, not just "I'd use Redux," is what reads as design skill rather than tool preference.
